rounds.verdict: A coherent and clean push-in, but no better enough than the baseline zoom to publish: the intended rise of the lift is barely separable from the camera move and the final frame is cramped at the barbell ends.
filmIssues: The move reads as a plain centred push-in: lifter and barbell have identical depth, drift and scale, so there is no distinct lift, reveal or parallax story beyond the camera zoom already credited as the baseline.
The combined camera zoom to 1.3 and layer scale to 1.12 pushes the barbell plates close to the left and right edges in the final frames, making the dwell frame feel cramped rather than triumphant.
The upward drift is too small relative to the zoom to register as the barbell being hoisted; the lifter mainly gets bigger, and his feet lose a clear planted relationship to the platform as he grows.
First frame is a good full opening picture and the last frame is legible and coherent, with no visible tearing, doubled edges or ghosting, and the lifter and barbell correctly stay together.

plan.rationale: A triumph in Rome: lifter and barbell rise together, growing as the camera tilts up and closes in, so the held lift becomes the silver-medal achievement.

rounds.verdict: Not publishable as-is: coherent and clean, but essentially a timid-then-rushed push-in whose final frame over-crops the platform and barbell instead of delivering a clear, held moment of triumph.
filmIssues: The move reads mainly as a centred push-in: the lifter and barbell grow, but they do not rise legibly against the crowd, trees and stadium, so the triumph is not clearly expressed beyond a plain zoom.

The pacing is uneven in the contact sheet — the first three frames change very little, then the framing jumps much larger between t=0.4 and t=0.6, so the lift feels late and rushed rather than a steady rise.

The final frame is too tight to dwell on: the platform is clipped at the bottom, the lifter's feet/platform base are pushed to the edge, and the barbell plates crowd the left and right edges. The opening wide frame is the better picture, the reverse of what the page needs.

Locking lifter and barbell together is correct — hands stay on the bar with no obvious tearing, doubling or ghosting — but giving both layers identical depth, drift and scale wastes the parallax; no separation is created from the background beyond the camera zoom.
The light-sweep is subtle and era-appropriate, but it cannot be discerned as purposeful sunlight in the frames and does not compensate for the weak rise.
